overview: Data profiling is the systematic, exploratory analysis of a dataset to compute descriptive statistics and structural patterns per column — including null/missing counts and percentages, distinct values and cardinality, min/max/mean/median/stddev, quantiles, most-frequent values, data type inference, string length distribution, pattern and regex inference, and cross-column relationships — producing a comprehensive baseline portrait of the data.

Profiling is the mandatory first step before writing data quality checks or setting monitoring thresholds: without knowing the real null rate, cardinality, and value distribution of a column, any threshold you choose is a guess; with profiling, thresholds become data-driven baselines rooted in actual observed behavior.

Modern data-profiling tools range from single-library solutions (ydata-profiling, whylogs) and framework-native profilers (Great Expectations auto-profiler, Amazon Deequ ColumnProfilerRunner) to warehouse-native SQL, cloud-managed services (AWS Glue DataBrew, Google Cloud Dataplex), and distributed engines (Apache Spark), each offering different trade-offs between depth, scale, and cost.

At large scale, exact profiling (full COUNT DISTINCT, exact quantiles) is replaced by approximate algorithms — HyperLogLog for cardinality, t-digest or reservoir sampling for quantiles — which cut compute cost dramatically while maintaining useful accuracy, making profiling viable on billion-row tables without full cluster scans.
learningObjectives: Explain what data profiling computes per column (nulls, cardinality, ranges, distributions, patterns, top values) and why each statistic matters for data quality.
Distinguish column profiling, cross-column profiling, and cross-table profiling (structure, content, and relationship discovery) and know when to use each.
Use ydata-profiling, SQL single-pass profiling queries, and Great Expectations or Amazon Deequ profilers to profile a dataset and interpret the outputs.
Translate profiling results into concrete data quality expectations, monitoring thresholds, and anomaly-detection baselines.
Apply approximate algorithms (HyperLogLog, t-digest, sampling) and engine-pushdown strategies to scale profiling to large datasets cost-effectively.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Data profiling is the process of examining a dataset from an existing data source and collecting metadata and statistical information about the structure, content, and relationships of that data — including per-column metrics (null count, distinct count, cardinality ratio, min/max/mean/median/stddev, quantile distribution, most-frequent values, type and format inference, string length distribution) and cross-column metrics (correlations, functional dependencies, candidate keys, and referential integrity between tables) — with the goal of understanding the data's quality, fitness, and characteristics before consuming or transforming it.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of profiling like a doctor's physical exam for your data. Before prescribing tests or treatments, the doctor measures all your vital signs — height, weight, blood pressure, heart rate, blood panel — to establish a healthy baseline. Data profiling does the same for every column in your table: it measures how often values are missing, how many unique values exist, what the min and max are, what values appear most often, and whether values match expected patterns like email or phone formats. Once you have that baseline portrait, you know what 'normal' looks like — so you can write targeted quality checks and instantly notice when something drifts.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early data quality research in the 1990s (Wang and Strong's 1996 framework) focused on dimensions like accuracy and completeness, but the mechanics of automated profiling were largely manual SQL queries run by database administrators. The data warehousing era popularized systematic metadata collection, and commercial ETL tools (Informatica, Talend) began bundling profiling modules in the 2000s. The big-data era brought distributed profiling via Apache Spark, and the modern open-source wave produced pandas-profiling (2016, later ydata-profiling), Amazon Deequ (2018), and Great Expectations (2018). The data observability movement (~2019-2020) framed profiling as a continuous activity rather than a one-time exercise, with tools like whylogs, Soda, and dbt-profiler embedding profiling into operational pipelines. Cloud providers added managed profiling services: AWS Glue DataBrew (2020) and Google Cloud Dataplex profiling (2021) brought no-code profiling to cloud warehouses.

whyItMatters.business: When a new data source arrives — a vendor feed, an acquired company's database, a third-party API — business teams cannot responsibly use it until its quality is understood. Profiling reveals whether customer IDs overlap, whether revenue figures are in dollars or cents, whether historical records are complete, and what percentage of critical fields are missing, allowing data teams to surface business risk before analysts build on shaky foundations.
whyItMatters.engineering: Profiling is the upstream input for every downstream quality activity: it tells you which columns need not-null checks, what distinct counts justify a uniqueness constraint, what the realistic value range is for a range check, and what regex pattern an identifier follows. Writing quality checks or setting monitoring thresholds without profiling is guesswork; profiling turns it into engineering.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of data sources and tables grows, manual column-by-column inspection is impossible. Automated profiling scans entire schemas, hundreds of columns, and millions of rows programmatically — and approximate algorithms (HyperLogLog, t-digest) make it feasible on warehouse-scale data without prohibitive compute cost.
whyItMatters.cost: Undetected data quality issues compound downstream: bad training data produces faulty ML models, bad metrics drive wrong business decisions, and data fixes after-the-fact are orders of magnitude more expensive than catching issues at source. Profiling during onboarding is cheap insurance that prevents expensive downstream rework.
whyItMatters.reliability: Profiling populates the baselines that drive anomaly detection and monitoring. A sudden drop in distinct customer_id count, a jump in null rate, or an unexpected new value in a controlled column — all detectable only because profiling established what the baseline distribution looked like — become the triggers for automated alerts long before a stakeholder notices an anomalous dashboard.

coreComponents.name: Column / Single-Column Profiler
coreComponents.definition: A component that computes per-column statistics independently: null count and null percentage, distinct count and cardinality ratio (distinct / row count), data type inference, min/max/mean/median/stddev, quantiles (p25/p50/p75/p95/p99), most-frequent (top-N) values and their frequencies, string length distribution (min/max/avg length), and regex pattern inference.
coreComponents.purpose: To produce a self-contained statistical portrait of each individual column, revealing its completeness, cardinality characteristics, value distribution, and format patterns without knowledge of other columns.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Execute a single-pass or parallel scan over each column, compute all relevant metrics, infer data type from values when schema is missing, detect obvious format patterns (email, phone, UUID, date), and emit a structured profile result per column.
coreComponents.examples: ydata-profiling column report, Deequ ColumnProfilerRunner per-column stats, SQL: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT col), MIN(col), MAX(col), AVG(col), STDDEV(col) per column in one pass.

coreComponents.name: Cross-Column / Relationship Profiler
coreComponents.definition: A component that analyzes relationships between pairs or groups of columns within a table: Pearson and Spearman correlations, functional dependencies (if column A determines column B, e.g., zip_code -> city), candidate-key detection (column combinations whose distinct count equals the row count), and mutual information / co-occurrence patterns.
coreComponents.purpose: To detect hidden structure and dependencies in data that single-column analysis misses: business keys are often composite, functional dependencies reveal normalization opportunities, and correlations surface features relevant for ML preprocessing.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compute pairwise column correlations, scan for functional dependencies using grouping and conditional distinct counts, identify columns or column combinations that could serve as unique identifiers, and flag suspicious or unexpected dependencies.
coreComponents.examples: ydata-profiling correlations tab, dbt-profiler functional dependency detection, SQL: SELECT zip_code, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS city_count FROM table GROUP BY zip_code HAVING city_count > 1 (functional dependency violation check).

coreComponents.name: Cross-Table / Referential Profiler
coreComponents.definition: A component that profiles relationships between columns across multiple tables: foreign-key candidate detection, referential integrity measurement (what percentage of FK values exist in the referenced table), overlap and join-key analysis between datasets, and schema comparison between source and target tables.
coreComponents.purpose: To validate join-ability before building pipelines, catch referential integrity violations that would produce incorrect joins or missing records, and detect candidate key relationships during data-source onboarding.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compare column value sets across tables, compute the percentage of foreign-key values that match primary-key values in the reference table, detect orphaned records, and identify potential join columns between new and existing datasets.
coreComponents.examples: SQL: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL (orphan detection); Deequ JoinConstraint analysis; ydata-profiling compare reports.

coreComponents.name: Statistical and Approximate Metric Engine
coreComponents.definition: The computation layer responsible for calculating exact or approximate statistical metrics at scale, including HyperLogLog for approximate distinct counts, t-digest or reservoir sampling for approximate quantiles, histogram binning for value distribution, and sampling strategies for full-table profiling on very large datasets.
coreComponents.purpose: To make profiling tractable on billion-row tables and multi-TB datasets where exact computation of every metric would require prohibitively expensive full scans, while preserving sufficient statistical accuracy for baseline and anomaly-detection purposes.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Choose between exact (COUNT DISTINCT) and approximate (HyperLogLog, APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT) computation based on table size and accuracy requirements, manage sampling rates for representative quantile estimation, push computation down to the warehouse or Spark engine, and report the estimation error alongside metric values.
coreComponents.examples: BigQuery APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(col), Redshift APPROXIMATE PERCENTILE_DISC, Spark approxCountDistinct(col, rsd=0.05), Python numpy percentile on a random 10% sample, t-digest quantile approximation.

internalWorking: A profiling run begins with a schema scan: the profiler reads column names, declared data types, and table row count from the catalog or information schema, establishing the skeleton of the profile before reading any data values.

For each column, a single SQL pass (or Spark aggregate) computes all numeric metrics in one scan: COUNT(*) for row count, COUNT(col) for non-null count (null count = row_count - non_null_count), COUNT(DISTINCT col) or APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT for cardinality, MIN/MAX/AVG/STDDEV for range and central tendency, PERCENTILE_CONT (or reservoir sampling) for quantiles, and a top-N frequency query using GROUP BY / ORDER BY COUNT DESC LIMIT N.

String columns receive additional analysis: string length distribution (MIN/MAX/AVG LENGTH(col)), regex pattern inference by testing candidate patterns (email, phone, UUID, date) against a sample and reporting the match percentage, and character encoding detection when applicable.

Cross-column analysis runs after individual column profiles are collected: the profiler computes a correlation matrix for numeric columns (Pearson/Spearman), runs functional-dependency checks by grouping on candidate-key columns and counting distinct values of dependent columns, and identifies composite-key candidates by testing column combinations whose combined distinct count equals the row count.

Results are assembled into a structured profile document (JSON, HTML report, or catalog metadata) containing per-column statistics, detected anomalies (e.g., a column declared INT containing non-numeric strings), cardinality classification (high/medium/low), format pattern match rates, cross-column dependencies, and summary-level quality indicators. This profile is persisted to feed downstream checks, monitoring baselines, and data catalog documentation.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source Table -> Schema Scan (catalog / information_schema) -> Single-Pass Column Scan (nulls, cardinality, min/max/avg/stddev, quantiles, top-N, string length, pattern matching) -> Cross-Column Analysis (correlations, functional dependencies, candidate keys) -> Cross-Table Analysis (referential integrity, join-key overlap) -> Profile Document (JSON / HTML / catalog metadata) -> Feed Quality Checks (thresholds, expectations) -> Feed Monitoring Baselines (anomaly detection) -> Data Catalog / Documentation
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A new vendor orders feed arrives in a staging table with 45 columns and an unknown schema; the team kicks off a profiling run before writing any transformations.

2. The schema scan reads column names and declared types from information_schema; the profiler detects 3 columns declared VARCHAR that contain numeric-only values (candidate for type coercion) and 1 column with no declared type.

3. The single-pass column scan executes a SQL query computing row_count, null_count, distinct_count (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT), min, max, avg, stddev, and top-5 values for all 45 columns in one warehouse query, returning results in under 60 seconds.

4. Column analysis reveals: order_id has cardinality ratio 1.00 (distinct count = row count), making it a candidate primary key; customer_id has 12% null rate (potential completeness issue); amount has a min of -500 (potential data error or refund encoding); order_status has only 6 distinct values (low cardinality, enum candidate); email column has 94% pattern match to the email regex.
5. Cross-column analysis reveals a functional dependency: zip_code -> city is violated in 3% of rows (inconsistency issue) and a strong correlation (0.87) between quantity and amount.

6. Cross-table analysis compares customer_id values in the vendor feed against the existing customers dimension table: 8.3% of customer_ids in the feed have no match in customers (orphaned foreign keys, which would cause silent join loss).

7. The completed profile is saved to the data catalog and used to auto-generate an initial Great Expectations expectation suite: not_null on order_id, null_rate < 15% on customer_id, amount between -600 and 100000, order_status in the observed 6 values, email regex match > 90%, and referential integrity check for customer_id.

keyTerminology.meaning: The number of distinct values in a column. High-cardinality columns (cardinality ratio near 1.0) are candidate keys or IDs; low-cardinality columns are likely categoricals or enums.
keyTerminology.importance: Cardinality drives decisions about primary-key constraints, indexing, partitioning strategies, and whether a column should be encoded as a categorical in ML features; misunderstanding cardinality leads to wrong schema design and failed joins.

keyTerminology.meaning: The fraction of rows where a column contains NULL: null_count / row_count. Expressed as a percentage (e.g., 4.3% null rate on email).
keyTerminology.importance: Null rate is the primary completeness metric for a column; it informs whether a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate and sets the baseline for monitoring — a sudden null-rate spike is one of the most common indicators of an upstream data pipeline failure.

keyTerminology.meaning: A probabilistic data structure and algorithm that approximates COUNT DISTINCT with configurable accuracy (typically ±1-2% error) using a fixed, small amount of memory, regardless of the dataset size.
keyTerminology.importance: Exact COUNT DISTINCT requires all distinct values to fit in memory or a full sort; HyperLogLog makes cardinality estimation on billion-row columns practical, and is natively implemented in BigQuery (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT), Redshift (APPROXIMATE COUNT DISTINCT), and Spark (approxCountDistinct).

keyTerminology.meaning: A relationship between columns where the value of column A uniquely determines the value of column B for all rows (e.g., zip_code -> city, product_id -> product_name). Violations indicate inconsistent or dirty data.
keyTerminology.importance: Detecting functional dependencies reveals normalization opportunities and data quality issues: if zip_code determines city in 97% of rows but not 3%, those 3% contain inconsistent data that will produce wrong results in joins and aggregations.

keyTerminology.meaning: The N most commonly occurring distinct values in a column and their occurrence counts and percentages (e.g., top-10 values for order_status, most common city in a shipping address column).
keyTerminology.importance: Top-N analysis reveals value skew, implicit enumerations, encoding anomalies (e.g., both 'N/A' and NULL used for missing), and whether the distribution is dominated by a single value (low informativeness) or spread across many values.

keyTerminology.meaning: The process of testing whether column values match known structural patterns (email, phone, UUID, date, ZIP code) and reporting the match percentage; some profilers also infer custom regex patterns from observed value structures.
keyTerminology.importance: Pattern matching surfaces format inconsistencies invisible to type checks — a VARCHAR column may contain a mix of valid emails and free-text entries; knowing 94% match the email regex tells you it is mostly an email column and flags the 6% as format violations worth inspecting.

importantConcepts.concept: Profiling as the Bootstrap for Quality Checks and Baselines
importantConcepts.explanation: Data profiling and data quality testing are deeply coupled: profiling provides the empirical observations that make quality expectations data-driven rather than guessed. When Great Expectations' UserConfigurableProfiler runs against a dataset, it automatically generates an expectation suite by observing the data — setting expect_column_values_to_not_be_null thresholds at the observed null rate, expect_column_values_to_be_in_set from the observed distinct values, and expect_column_values_to_be_between from the observed min/max. The same logic applies to monitoring: a null-rate anomaly detector only knows what threshold to flag as anomalous because profiling established the historical baseline. Without profiling, thresholds are either too tight (causing false alarms and alert fatigue) or too loose (missing real issues). Profiling is therefore not optional prep work but the quantitative foundation on which the entire quality and observability stack is built.

importantConcepts.concept: Structure Discovery, Content Discovery, and Relationship Discovery
importantConcepts.explanation: Data profiling spans three distinct layers of investigation. Structure discovery examines the schema itself: column names, declared data types, nullability constraints, and how the observed type of values compares to the declared type (e.g., a column declared FLOAT that contains only integers, or a VARCHAR column whose values are all numeric). Content discovery examines the actual values: completeness (null rates), cardinality, value distributions, statistical moments (mean, stddev, quantiles), top-N frequencies, string lengths, and format patterns. Relationship discovery examines how columns and tables relate: pairwise correlations, functional dependencies, candidate-key detection, referential integrity between tables, and join-key overlap analysis. Mature profiling runs all three layers and combines their outputs into a unified profile that tells the full story of a dataset before any pipeline is built on it.

importantConcepts.concept: Approximate vs. Exact Profiling at Scale
importantConcepts.explanation: Exact profiling — computing COUNT DISTINCT, exact quantiles, and full histograms — requires either sorting all values or maintaining them in memory, which becomes cost-prohibitive on tables with hundreds of millions or billions of rows. Approximate algorithms address this: HyperLogLog computes distinct counts with ~1% relative error using kilobytes of memory regardless of data size; t-digest or reservoir sampling computes approximate quantiles with configurable accuracy; and random sampling (e.g., 10% of rows) allows full-column profiling on a representative subset. Modern warehouses expose these natively: BigQuery APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, Redshift APPROXIMATE PERCENTILE_DISC, Snowflake APPROX_PERCENTILE, and Spark approxCountDistinct. A practical profiling strategy uses approximate algorithms for large tables, exact computation for small tables or high-value columns, and sampling for distribution-intensive metrics like histograms and correlation matrices. The accuracy trade-off is well-understood and documented alongside results.

One of the highest-value uses of profiling is understanding a new, unfamiliar data source before building pipelines on it. When a vendor delivers a new feed, a legacy database is migrated, or a third-party API is integrated, the receiving data team has no ground truth about the data's shape and quality. Profiling the raw source answers critical questions: Which columns can serve as a join key? What is the actual null rate on columns the business considers mandatory? Are the declared data types accurate? Do values conform to expected formats? Are there hidden enumerations in VARCHAR columns? Are there referential integrity relationships to existing tables? Answering these questions through profiling before writing transformations prevents the common pattern of discovering a data quality problem months later when a downstream consumer notices wrong results.

One-time profiling at onboarding establishes an initial baseline, but data distributions, null rates, and cardinality evolve as the source system changes. Continuous profiling — running a lightweight profile on each new batch or daily partition and persisting the per-column metrics to a history table — enables trend analysis and anomaly detection over time. If the null rate on customer_email rises from 2% to 15% over three consecutive days, incremental profiling catches that drift and triggers an alert; a one-time profile would not. Tools like whylogs are specifically designed for this use case, computing statistical summaries per batch that can be compared over time. This continuous-profiling pattern is the foundation of the data observability approach: rather than just checking whether today's values pass static thresholds, you track how the distribution is changing and alert on meaningful deviation from the established baseline.

variationsAndTypes: **Column / single-column profiling:** per-column statistics in isolation — null rate, cardinality, min/max/mean/stddev, quantiles, top-N values, string length, pattern match — the foundation of every profiling run.

**Cross-column / intra-table profiling:** pairwise correlations (Pearson, Spearman, phi for categoricals), functional dependency detection, conditional distributions, and composite candidate-key identification within a single table.

**Cross-table / referential profiling:** foreign-key candidate detection, referential integrity measurement (orphan rate), join-key overlap analysis, and schema comparison between source and target tables.
**Structure profiling:** focuses on schema-level metadata — declared vs. inferred types, nullability constraints, naming conventions, column count, and schema drift detection between versions.
**Content profiling:** focuses on value-level analysis — distributions, frequencies, patterns, outliers, and data anomalies within the actual column values.
**Relationship profiling:** focuses on dependencies and associations between columns or tables — correlations, functional dependencies, referential integrity, and candidate keys.

**Incremental / continuous profiling:** runs a lightweight column profile on each new batch or partition and persists metrics over time to enable trend analysis, drift detection, and anomaly-based alerting.
advantages: **Data-driven quality checks:** Profiling replaces guesswork with empirical evidence when setting null-rate thresholds, cardinality expectations, and value-range bounds, producing checks that are accurate and minimally noisy from day one.

**Early issue discovery:** Profiling a new source before pipeline construction surfaces encoding anomalies, unexpected nulls, type mismatches, referential integrity gaps, and format inconsistencies before any downstream work is built on the data.

**Auto-generated expectations and baselines:** Great Expectations UserConfigurableProfiler and Deequ ColumnProfilerRunner can translate a profiling run directly into an initial expectation suite or constraint set, dramatically accelerating quality-check authoring.

**Feeds data catalog and documentation:** Profile statistics (null rates, cardinality, value distributions, format patterns) populate data catalog metadata, making datasets self-documenting and helping downstream consumers understand data without needing to query it themselves.

**Supports anomaly detection and monitoring:** Persisting column-level metrics over time creates the historical baseline against which anomaly detectors alert — a sudden null-rate jump or cardinality collapse is only detectable because earlier profiles established the normal range.
disadvantages: **Full-scan cost:** Comprehensive profiling of a large table (especially exact COUNT DISTINCT and quantiles) requires a full-table scan, which is expensive in cloud warehouses billed by bytes scanned; approximate algorithms and sampling mitigate but do not eliminate this cost.

**Profiling is a snapshot, not a guarantee:** A profile reflects the data at the moment of the scan; a source system can deliver clean data during profiling and dirty data thereafter; profiling does not validate ongoing quality, only establishes a baseline.

**Sensitive data exposure:** Profile outputs containing top-N values, sample rows, or string patterns may inadvertently expose PII (names, emails, SSNs appearing in top-value lists); profiling systems need masking and access controls.

**Misinterpreted cardinality:** High cardinality does not always mean a column is a primary key (e.g., free-text comments have high cardinality but are not keys); and low cardinality does not mean the column is an enum (e.g., a column with 5 distinct values in a small sample may have many more in production data).

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Run a full profiling pass whenever onboarding a new data source, before writing quality checks or transformations, after a significant schema or volume change in a source system, and before migrating data to a new warehouse or schema design. Run continuous incremental profiling on high-value production tables to feed monitoring baselines and anomaly detection.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid full exact profiling on extremely large tables in cost-sensitive warehouse environments without first applying sampling or approximate algorithms; avoid profiling transient intermediate tables that exist only within a single pipeline run and carry no business meaning; and avoid storing profiling outputs containing raw top-N values from PII-sensitive columns without masking.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Data profiling is like a real-estate inspector's pre-purchase survey of a house. Before you sign a contract (build a pipeline), the inspector measures every room (column), notes what materials were used (data types), checks for cracks or moisture (null values, anomalies), tests whether doors and windows open correctly (format patterns), confirms the plumbing connects to the mains (referential integrity), and compares the layout to the blueprint (declared schema vs. actual content). The inspection report doesn't fix anything — it tells you exactly what you're buying so you can decide whether to proceed, negotiate repair obligations (define quality checks), and know what to monitor once you move in (set anomaly baselines).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Profiling is only useful when you don't know the data; for familiar sources you can skip it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Familiar sources change over time — source systems are updated, new teams modify ETL, upstream encodings shift. Running profiling on each new batch as continuous profiling is the only way to detect when a 'known' source starts delivering unexpected distributions, new null patterns, or schema changes. Many real production incidents involve a source that was 'known' but changed silently.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A column with no nulls and all unique values doesn't need profiling.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Zero-null, fully-unique columns can still contain format anomalies (e.g., order IDs mixing two different ID formats from merged systems), value outliers (a single row with order_amount = 9999999 that is a test record), or distribution shifts (IDs incrementing at a much faster rate than expected, signaling a load duplication). Profiling reveals all of these; absence of nulls and uniqueness are necessary but not sufficient quality signals.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Profiling and data quality testing are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Profiling is exploratory and descriptive — it computes statistics about what the data actually looks like. Testing is prescriptive — it asserts what the data should look like and fails when reality diverges from expectation. Profiling feeds testing by providing the empirical observations that make expectations accurate, but they serve different roles: profiling is discovery, testing is enforcement. Running only profiling without quality checks means issues are observed but never blocked.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Push profiling computation down to the warehouse or Spark engine using native aggregate functions; use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HyperLogLog) for cardinality on large tables; use APPROX_PERCENTILE or reservoir sampling for quantiles; partition profiling scans by date so only the current partition is scanned for incremental profiling jobs rather than the full table history.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make profiling jobs idempotent — if a profiling run fails mid-way, re-running it should produce the same result without duplicating metrics history entries. Version profiling configurations (which columns to profile, sampling rates, thresholds) alongside pipeline code so changes are auditable.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Design profiling jobs to tolerate individual column failures without aborting the entire run — if an exotic data type on one column causes a computation error, log the failure for that column, skip it, and proceed with the rest. Persisting partial profile results is more useful than losing the entire run.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor the profiling jobs themselves: track whether profiling ran on schedule, whether row counts differ significantly from the previous run, whether any column's null rate or cardinality changed beyond a configurable sensitivity threshold. Alert on profiling job failures as a first-class data reliability signal.
productionConsiderations.security: Apply column-level masking or exclusion for PII columns in profiling outputs: top-N values for an email column will contain real email addresses; a name column's top values may reveal real customer names. Use separate access controls for raw profile outputs (internal engineering use) versus catalog-facing summaries (broader audience). Ensure profiling jobs run with least-privilege credentials.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Schedule full profiling scans during off-peak warehouse hours to avoid competing with production queries; use sampling (10-20% random sample) for expensive distribution metrics on very large tables; run cheap metrics (nulls, row count, min/max) on every batch but schedule expensive metrics (exact distinct counts, full histograms, cross-column correlations) on a weekly or monthly cadence; cache profiling results and avoid re-scanning unchanged partitions.
productionConsiderations.performance: Compute all per-column aggregate metrics in a single SQL pass to minimize the number of table scans; use columnar storage formats (Parquet, ORC) which allow the warehouse to read only the profiled columns rather than the entire row; parallelize Spark profiling across multiple columns and partitions simultaneously using DataFrame aggregate API rather than sequential column loops.

codeExamples.title: Warehouse-Native Single-Pass SQL Column Profiler
codeExamples.overview: A single SQL query that profiles a table in one scan, computing row count, per-column null counts, approximate distinct counts (HyperLogLog), min/max/avg/stddev, and a separate top-N frequency query — a pattern usable in Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, or any ANSI-SQL warehouse.
codeExamples.code:
-- Step 1: Single-pass column profile for the orders table
-- Replace APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT with COUNT(DISTINCT ...) for exact counts
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                                  AS row_count,

  -- order_id: completeness + cardinality
  COUNT(order_id)                           AS order_id_non_null,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(order_id)                AS order_id_null_count,
  ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(order_id)) / COUNT(*), 2) AS order_id_null_pct,
  APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(order_id)           AS order_id_approx_distinct,

  -- customer_id: completeness + cardinality
  COUNT(customer_id)                        AS customer_id_non_null,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)             AS customer_id_null_count,
  ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)) / COUNT(*), 2) AS customer_id_null_pct,
  APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(customer_id)        AS customer_id_approx_distinct,

  -- amount: range + distribution
  MIN(amount)                               AS amount_min,
  MAX(amount)                               AS amount_max,
  ROUND(AVG(amount), 4)                     AS amount_avg,
  ROUND(STDDEV(amount), 4)                  AS amount_stddev,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(amount)                  AS amount_null_count,

  -- order_status: completeness + cardinality (enum)
  COUNT(order_status)                       AS order_status_non_null,
  APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(order_status)       AS order_status_distinct,

  -- email: completeness + pattern match
  COUNT(email)                              AS email_non_null,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(email)                   AS email_null_count,
  ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(email)) / COUNT(*), 2) AS email_null_pct,
  -- Pattern match: fraction of emails matching basic email regex (Snowflake syntax)
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN email REGEXP '^[^@]+@[^@]+\\.[^@]+$' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
        / NULLIF(COUNT(email), 0), 2)        AS email_pattern_match_pct,

  -- Freshness
  MAX(created_at)                           AS latest_created_at,
  DATEDIFF('hour', MAX(created_at), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) AS hours_since_latest

FROM staging.orders
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';  -- partition filter


-- Step 2: Top-5 values for order_status (separate query per categorical column)
SELECT
  order_status,
  COUNT(*)                                  AS frequency,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_total
FROM staging.orders
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY order_status
ORDER BY frequency DESC
LIMIT 5;
codeExamples.breakdown: Step 1 executes a single aggregation pass over the table computing all per-column metrics: null_count and null_pct use COUNT(*) - COUNT(col) (COUNT ignores NULLs); APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT uses HyperLogLog for cardinality with ~1% error at much lower cost than exact COUNT DISTINCT; MIN/MAX/AVG/STDDEV compute range and distribution for numeric columns; the REGEXP CASE WHEN computes the email pattern match percentage inline; and DATEDIFF measures data freshness. The INTERVAL filter pushes the scan to a single partition. Step 2 uses a window function (SUM OVER ()) to compute percentage of total alongside raw frequency counts for the categorical column, identifying the dominant values and any unexpected value appearing in the distribution.

codeExamples.title: ydata-profiling: Automated HTML Profile Report and Key Statistics
codeExamples.overview: Use ydata-profiling (formerly pandas-profiling) to generate a comprehensive HTML profile report from a pandas DataFrame, extract key per-column statistics programmatically, and identify data quality issues surfaced by the profiler.
codeExamples.code:
import pandas as pd
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport
import json

# Load data (replace with your actual source: read_parquet, read_csv, etc.)
df = pd.read_parquet("s3://data-lake/staging/orders/2024-01-15/orders.parquet")

print(f"Dataset shape: {df.shape[0]:,} rows x {df.shape[1]} columns")

# --- Generate a full profile report ---
# minimal=True is faster for large DataFrames; set to False for full correlations
profile = ProfileReport(
    df,
    title="Orders Staging Table Profile - 2024-01-15",
    explorative=True,       # include advanced stats
    correlations={
        "pearson": {"calculate": True},
        "spearman": {"calculate": True},
        "cramers": {"calculate": True},   # categorical associations
    },
    missing_diagrams={
        "heatmap": True,     # co-occurrence of missing values
    },
    samples={"head": 5, "tail": 5},
    progress_bar=True,
)

# Save the interactive HTML report
profile.to_file("orders_profile_2024-01-15.html")
print("Profile report saved to orders_profile_2024-01-15.html")

# --- Extract key statistics programmatically ---
# get_description() returns a nested dict with all profile data
desc = profile.get_description()

print("\n=== Per-Column Profile Summary ===")
print(f"{'Column':<20} {'Type':<12} {'Null %':>8} {'Distinct':>10} {'Cardinality':>12}")
print("-" * 65)

for col_name, col_stats in desc.variables.items():
    null_pct  = round(col_stats.get("p_missing", 0) * 100, 2)
    n_distinct = col_stats.get("n_distinct", "N/A")
    n_rows    = desc.table["n"]
    cardinality = round(n_distinct / n_rows, 4) if isinstance(n_distinct, int) else "N/A"
    col_type  = col_stats.get("type", "unknown")
    print(f"{col_name:<20} {col_type:<12} {null_pct:>7.2f}% {str(n_distinct):>10} {str(cardinality):>12}")

# --- Flag columns with quality issues ---
print("\n=== Quality Issues Detected ===")
for col_name, col_stats in desc.variables.items():
    null_pct   = col_stats.get("p_missing", 0) * 100
    n_distinct = col_stats.get("n_distinct", 0)
    n_rows     = desc.table["n"]

    if null_pct > 5:
        print(f"  HIGH NULL RATE  : {col_name} -> {null_pct:.2f}% missing")

    if isinstance(n_distinct, int) and n_rows > 0:
        card_ratio = n_distinct / n_rows
        # Warn if a column claimed to be an ID has cardinality < 0.99
        if "id" in col_name.lower() and card_ratio < 0.99:
            print(f"  LOW CARDINALITY : {col_name} -> cardinality ratio {card_ratio:.4f} (possible duplicates)")

# --- Print numeric column stats ---
print("\n=== Numeric Column Descriptive Stats ===")
numeric_cols = [c for c, s in desc.variables.items() if s.get("type") == "Numeric"]
for col in numeric_cols:
    s = desc.variables[col]
    print(f"{col}: min={s.get('min')}, max={s.get('max')}, "
          f"mean={round(s.get('mean', 0), 4)}, stddev={round(s.get('std', 0), 4)}, "
          f"p25={s.get('25%')}, p50={s.get('50%')}, p75={s.get('75%')}")

codeExamples.title: From-Scratch Column Profiler Function with Structured Output
codeExamples.overview: A reusable Python function that profiles a pandas DataFrame and returns a structured profile dictionary per column — null percentage, distinct count, cardinality ratio, min/max/mean, top-5 values — suitable for logging to a profiling history store or feeding into automated threshold generation.
codeExamples.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from typing import Any


def profile_dataframe(df: pd.DataFrame, top_n: int = 5) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Profile every column in a DataFrame.
    Returns a dict: { column_name -> column_profile_dict }
    """
    row_count = len(df)
    profile: dict[str, Any] = {
        "_metadata": {
            "row_count": row_count,
            "column_count": len(df.columns),
            "total_cells": row_count * len(df.columns),
        }
    }

    for col in df.columns:
        series = df[col]
        null_count  = int(series.isna().sum())
        non_null    = series.dropna()
        distinct    = int(series.nunique(dropna=False))   # includes NULL as a distinct value if present
        distinct_nn = int(non_null.nunique())             # distinct non-null values

        col_profile: dict[str, Any] = {
            "dtype":         str(series.dtype),
            "null_count":    null_count,
            "null_pct":      round(100.0 * null_count / row_count, 4) if row_count else 0.0,
            "distinct_count": distinct_nn,
            "cardinality_ratio": round(distinct_nn / row_count, 6) if row_count else 0.0,
        }

        # Numeric stats
        if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(series):
            col_profile.update({
                "min":    float(non_null.min())    if len(non_null) else None,
                "max":    float(non_null.max())    if len(non_null) else None,
                "mean":   round(float(non_null.mean()), 6)   if len(non_null) else None,
                "median": round(float(non_null.median()), 6) if len(non_null) else None,
                "stddev": round(float(non_null.std()), 6)    if len(non_null) else None,
                "p25":    round(float(np.percentile(non_null, 25)), 6) if len(non_null) else None,
                "p75":    round(float(np.percentile(non_null, 75)), 6) if len(non_null) else None,
                "p99":    round(float(np.percentile(non_null, 99)), 6) if len(non_null) else None,
                "negative_count": int((non_null < 0).sum()),
            })

        # String / object stats
        if pd.api.types.is_string_dtype(series) or series.dtype == object:
            str_series = non_null.astype(str)
            lengths = str_series.str.len()
            col_profile.update({
                "min_length":  int(lengths.min())  if len(lengths) else None,
                "max_length":  int(lengths.max())  if len(lengths) else None,
                "mean_length": round(float(lengths.mean()), 2) if len(lengths) else None,
            })
            # Pattern checks
            email_pattern = r"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$"
            col_profile["email_match_pct"] = round(
                100.0 * str_series.str.match(email_pattern).sum() / len(str_series), 2
            ) if len(str_series) else 0.0

        # Top-N value frequencies
        top_values = (
            series.value_counts(dropna=False)
            .head(top_n)
            .reset_index()
        )
        top_values.columns = ["value", "count"]
        top_values["pct"] = round(100.0 * top_values["count"] / row_count, 2)
        col_profile["top_values"] = top_values.to_dict(orient="records")

        profile[col] = col_profile

    return profile


# --- Example usage ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Synthetic sample data
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "order_id":     list(range(1, 10001)),
        "customer_id":  [None if i % 31 == 0 else (i % 9500) for i in range(10000)],
        "amount":       np.random.exponential(scale=120, size=10000).round(2),
        "order_status": np.random.choice(["placed","shipped","delivered","cancelled"], 10000),
        "email":        [f"user{i}@example.com" if i % 17 != 0 else "INVALID_EMAIL" for i in range(10000)],
    })

    result = profile_dataframe(df, top_n=5)

    # Print summary
    print(f"Profiled {result['_metadata']['row_count']:,} rows x "
          f"{result['_metadata']['column_count']} columns\n")

    for col, stats in result.items():
        if col == "_metadata":
            continue
        print(f"Column: {col}")
        print(f"  dtype={stats['dtype']}, null_pct={stats['null_pct']}%, "
              f"distinct={stats['distinct_count']}, cardinality={stats['cardinality_ratio']}")
        if "mean" in stats:
            print(f"  min={stats['min']}, max={stats['max']}, "
                  f"mean={stats['mean']}, stddev={stats['stddev']}")
        if "email_match_pct" in stats:
            print(f"  email_match_pct={stats['email_match_pct']}%")
        print(f"  top_values: {stats['top_values'][:3]}")
        print()

Numeric columns get min/max/mean/median/stddev and key percentiles (p25/p75/p99) computed via numpy.percentile; negative_count flags columns that should be non-negative but contain negative values. String/object columns get string length distribution (min/max/mean length) and an email pattern match percentage. Top-N values use value_counts(dropna=False) which correctly counts NaN as a distinct value category, critical for understanding whether NULL appears as an explicit top value. The result dict is directly JSON-serializable (after converting numpy types) and suitable for insertion into a profiling history table.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A fintech company is onboarding a new payment processor's transaction feed that will replace their legacy processor. Before migrating production traffic, the data team must understand the new feed's structure and quality, detect any fields that are missing, malformed, or inconsistently populated, identify whether the feed's transaction IDs are joinable with the existing customer and merchant dimension tables, and generate a baseline expectation suite so the production pipeline has automated quality gates from day one.
endToEndExample.inputData: A daily Parquet file delivered to an S3 staging bucket: transactions from the new payment processor, approximately 2.1 million rows per day, 38 columns including transaction_id, customer_id, merchant_id, amount, currency, transaction_type, status, card_last4, country_code, created_at, and 28 additional metadata columns.
endToEndExample.architecture: S3 staging bucket -> Profiling job (Spark on EMR or warehouse SQL) -> Profile document (JSON persisted to S3 and data catalog) -> Cross-table referential profiling against customers and merchants dimensions -> Profile-driven expectation suite generation (Great Expectations UserConfigurableProfiler) -> Pipeline CI validation (GE checkpoint on staging data) -> Production ingestion pipeline with embedded quality gate.
processingSteps: 1. Schema scan: read Parquet metadata via pyarrow.parquet.read_schema() to extract declared column names and types without loading data; compare against the expected schema contract from the payment processor's API documentation — identify 3 undocumented columns and 2 type mismatches (amount declared as STRING but containing numeric values; created_at declared as INT but containing Unix timestamps).

2. Single-pass column profiling: run a Spark aggregate over all 38 columns in one job computing null counts, approxCountDistinct (HyperLogLog with 1% error), min/max/avg/stddev for numerics, and top-5 value frequencies for categoricals; total scan time: 4m 12s on 2.1M rows.

3. Profiling analysis: critical findings: transaction_id has cardinality ratio 1.0 (valid PK candidate); customer_id has 6.8% null rate (higher than the legacy feed's 0.3% — potential data contract violation); currency column has 4 distinct values but includes 'XXX' (unknown currency code) in 0.4% of rows; country_code has 12 values but one ('ZZ') is not a valid ISO 3166 code; amount has a min of 0.00 (valid) and a max of 250000.00 with stddev of 842 (long-tail distribution, expected for payments).

4. Cross-table referential profiling: compare customer_id values in the new feed against the customers dimension: 11.2% of customer_ids have no match (significantly higher than the legacy feed's 1.8%); compare merchant_id against the merchants dimension: 0.3% orphan rate (acceptable). Root cause investigation: the payment processor uses a different customer ID namespace for one product line (identified via the 'ZZ' country code correlation — ZZ transactions have 98% orphan rate, confirming a scoped data issue).

5. Cross-column analysis: detect functional dependency: country_code -> currency holds for 99.6% of rows (expected) but 0.4% violate it (the 'XXX' currency rows); strong correlation (0.92) between amount and is_international_flag (expected); transaction_type and status have a functional dependency that holds 99.9% of rows (refunds always have status='reversed').

6. Profile-driven expectation generation: the Great Expectations UserConfigurableProfiler is run against the profile results to auto-generate an expectation suite: expect_column_values_to_not_be_null(transaction_id), expect_column_values_to_be_unique(transaction_id), expect_column_values_to_be_between(amount, 0, 300000), expect_column_values_to_be_in_set(currency, ['USD','EUR','GBP','CAD']), expect_column_values_to_match_regex(created_at, timestamp regex), null rate on customer_id < 8% (profiled baseline + buffer), country_code in observed valid set minus 'ZZ'.

7. Findings documented and shared: profiling report saved to the data catalog with per-column statistics, quality issue annotations, referential integrity findings, and the auto-generated expectation suite; data team meets with the payment processor to resolve the customer ID namespace mismatch and 'XXX'/'ZZ' encoding issues before production cutover.
endToEndExample.output: A structured JSON profile document covering all 38 columns with per-column statistics and quality flags; an annotated findings report identifying 5 data quality issues; a Great Expectations expectation suite with 22 expectations ready for production pipeline integration; referential integrity analysis showing the customer ID namespace mismatch; and a recommendation to delay production cutover until the 11.2% orphan rate is resolved.
endToEndExample.monitoring: After production onboarding, the profiling job runs daily on each new batch; per-column metrics (null rates, distinct counts, top values, min/max/avg) are written to a profiling_history table. A monitoring job compares today's metrics to the 30-day rolling baseline and alerts if customer_id null rate rises above the 8% threshold, currency distinct count changes (new or removed currency codes), or transaction volume deviates more than 20% from the 7-day moving average.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If the daily Parquet file is missing, the profiling job fails with a clear error and alerts the data owner; the production pipeline is blocked until profiling succeeds. If profiling detects that transaction_id cardinality ratio drops below 0.999 (indicating duplicates in the feed), the batch is quarantined and the payment processor is notified. Individual column profiling failures (e.g., an unexpected type on a new column) are logged with the column name and error type but do not abort the full profiling run.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The payment processor feed was onboarded with full transparency about its quality characteristics. Five data quality issues were identified and resolved before production cutover. The auto-generated expectation suite provided a quality gate that caught three additional feed anomalies in the first month of production (a temporary currency code introduced by the processor, a batch with elevated null customer_ids, and a day where the feed was redelivered causing duplicates). Mean time to detection for feed issues dropped from the legacy system's average of 18 hours (when detected by stakeholders) to under 30 minutes via automated profiling alerts.
