productionDeepDive.scalability: At production scale (tables with hundreds of millions to billions of rows), exact profiling metrics become cost-prohibitive: a full COUNT DISTINCT on a 1B-row table in BigQuery can cost $5-10 per query. The solution is a tiered approach: use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HyperLogLog, ~1% relative error) for cardinality on all tables above 10M rows; use APPROX_PERCENTILE or reservoir sampling for quantiles; partition-filter all profiling scans to the current incremental window rather than the full table; and profile at the partition level (daily slice) rather than the full table for incremental pipelines. Spark's approxCountDistinct(col, relativeSD=0.05) and approxQuantile(col, probabilities, relativeError) expose the same approximate algorithms on distributed data. For very wide tables (100+ columns), generate the profiling SQL programmatically from information_schema metadata and batch columns into groups to avoid single-query timeout limits.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Profiling jobs must be idempotent: writing profile results to a history table should use an UPSERT (merge on run_date + table_name + column_name) rather than an INSERT so reruns on failure don't duplicate rows. Individual column profiling failures (e.g., an unsupported type or a column added after job configuration) should be caught per-column and logged without aborting the full profiling run — partial profiles are more useful than no profile. For distributed Spark profiling, configure checkpointing so the job can resume from the last completed partition rather than restarting from scratch after a cluster preemption.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Profiling is typically a batch job on an orchestrated schedule (Airflow, Prefect, dbt run) rather than a real-time service, so HA means reliable scheduling and retries rather than active-passive failover. Configure 2-3 automatic retries with exponential backoff for transient warehouse or Spark failures. Store profiling results in durable, replicated storage (S3, GCS, warehouse tables) rather than local disk. If profiling fails for multiple consecutive runs, escalate the alert from data-team notification to an on-call incident, because missing profiling baselines will eventually degrade anomaly-detection accuracy.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Profiling history tables are the source of truth for 'what normal looks like' for anomaly detection. Back them up on the same schedule as your analytical tables and include them in warehouse disaster recovery plans. If profiling history is lost, the anomaly detection system loses its baselines and will generate excessive alerts or miss issues until the history is rebuilt. For new environments (DR region, new warehouse), seed the profiling history by replaying the last 30-90 days of historical data through the profiling job before enabling anomaly detection to prevent false alerts from an empty baseline.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Consolidate all per-column aggregate metrics into a single SQL query (one table scan) rather than issuing one query per column or per metric — this is the single highest-impact optimization for warehouse-based profiling. Use columnar storage formats (Parquet, ORC) and query only the columns being profiled rather than SELECT * (warehouse engines read only referenced columns from columnar formats). For Spark profiling, use DataFrame.agg() with a dict of aggregate expressions to compute all column metrics in one Spark job pass. Profile smaller incremental windows (today's partition) rather than the full table for operational efficiency, and run full-table baseline refreshes on a weekly or monthly cadence. Cache the information_schema query (column list, data types) and reuse it across profiling runs.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: In pay-per-query warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Athena), the biggest cost lever is scan reduction: always apply a partition filter to limit profiling to the relevant incremental window. Use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT instead of COUNT DISTINCT on large columns — it typically reduces compute by 10-100x. Tier profiling depth by table importance: run full profiling (all metrics, correlations, cross-table checks) on critical production tables; run lightweight profiling (only null count, row count, and min/max) on intermediate or transient tables. Schedule profiling jobs during off-peak hours when reserved-capacity pricing or warehouse auto-suspend reduces costs. For S3/Parquet data, use column pushdown with pyarrow to read only the profiled columns rather than loading the full dataset into memory.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Profile outputs, especially top-N value lists, can expose sensitive data: the top-5 values for a customer_name column will be real customer names; top values for a payment_card_hash column could expose hash patterns. Apply column-level exclusion lists in profiling configuration to skip columns containing PII (name, SSN, card numbers, health data) from top-N value output. Use tokenized or masked representations in catalog-facing profile summaries. Ensure profiling jobs run under service account credentials with SELECT-only access, not data-pipeline or admin roles. Apply row-level security on profiling history tables so engineers only see profiling stats for datasets they are authorized to access.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Monitor the profiling infrastructure itself as a first-class concern: alert if a profiling job fails (profiling SLA breach), if a table was not profiled within the expected window, or if the profiling job's own run time increases significantly (may indicate a growing table requiring scaling). Track per-column metric history in a time-series table and run a lightweight anomaly detection job after each profiling run: flag columns where null_pct changed by more than 2 percentage points, distinct_count dropped by more than 5%, or row_count deviated more than 20% from the 7-day average. Route anomaly alerts to the table owner with the column name, the metric, today's value, and the expected range — not a raw metric dump.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Profiling results themselves should be validated before being trusted: check that row_count in the profiling output matches the row count reported by the warehouse's table metadata (they should be identical for a full scan); check that null_pct is between 0 and 100; check that distinct_count <= row_count; check that min <= median <= max for numeric columns. These meta-validations detect bugs in profiling code or partial-scan failures that could seed wrong baselines into anomaly detection. Also validate that the profiling job covered all expected columns by comparing the profiled column list against information_schema — new columns added to the source without updating the profiling configuration will be silently missed.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log every profiling run with: run_id, table_name, run_date, row_count, column_count, run_duration_seconds, and a per-column JSON blob of computed statistics. Log profiling failures with the column name, error type, and stack trace so debugging is actionable. For alerting, distinguish between profiling job failure alerts (the infrastructure did not run — high severity, blocks downstream quality checks) and profiling anomaly alerts (the data looks different from baseline — medium severity, needs investigation). Route anomaly alerts only to the dataset owner, not a global channel, to avoid alert fatigue. Include the historical baseline value alongside the current value in every alert so the recipient can assess severity without needing to query the profiling history table themselves.

recommendedPractices: **Profile before you pipeline:** always run a full profiling pass on a new data source before writing any transformations or quality checks — profiling results should drive every threshold, constraint, and expectation in the downstream pipeline.

**Persist profile history:** store per-column profiling metrics in a time-series history table (run_date, table_name, column_name, metric, value) to enable trend analysis, drift detection, and anomaly detection over time — a single profile snapshot has limited value without history to compare against.

**Use approximate algorithms at scale:** default to APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HyperLogLog) for cardinality and approximate quantile functions for distribution metrics on tables above 10M rows; exact computation is only needed when the specific downstream use case requires exactness.

**Partition-filter all profiling scans:** always apply a date or partition filter to profiling queries so incremental runs scan only the new data window, not the full table history; reserve full-table profiling for baseline refreshes on a weekly or monthly cadence.

**Translate profiling to expectations:** after every profiling run, generate or update quality expectations and monitoring thresholds from the observed statistics — profiling that does not feed downstream checks or baselines is documentation, not engineering.
engineeringStandards: Profiling configurations (which tables, which columns, sampling rates, excluded PII columns) are version-controlled in the same repository as pipeline and transformation code.
Profiling jobs run on every new batch for critical tables and produce a pass/fail signal that gates downstream pipeline execution.

Profile results are written to a profiling history table with a defined schema (run_id, run_date, table_name, column_name, metric_name, metric_value) — ad-hoc profile outputs that are not persisted do not count as production profiling.
PII columns are explicitly listed in profiling configuration exclusion lists so top-N value outputs never contain sensitive data in any environment.
designRecommendations: Design profiling as a single-pass SQL or Spark aggregate that computes all per-column metrics in one table scan — never issue one query per column or per metric on the same table.

Separate profiling (compute statistics about the data) from validation (assert the data meets expectations) in the pipeline DAG — profiling feeds validation, but they serve different purposes and should be independently triggerable and observable.

Include a cross-table referential profiling step whenever a new source is onboarded or after a major source schema change to detect FK orphan rates before they cause silent join loss in downstream tables.

Design the profiling history table to support time-series queries: index on (table_name, column_name, run_date) and store metric_value as a FLOAT with a separate metric_name VARCHAR column so new metrics can be added without schema changes.
namingConventions: Name profiling history tables: `dq_profiling_history` or `<schema>_profiling_history`, with columns: run_id, run_date, table_name, column_name, metric_name, metric_value, is_approximate.
Name profiling configuration files: `<table>_profiling_config.yaml` containing column exclusions, sampling rates, and metric selections.
Name profiling anomaly alert metric: `<table>__<column>__<metric>_anomaly`, e.g., `orders__customer_id__null_pct_anomaly`.
documentationStandards: Document each profiling run's purpose, the table and partition profiled, the sampling rate if any, and the key findings in the data catalog entry for the table.
Document PII column exclusions explicitly in profiling configuration with a justification comment so future engineers understand why certain columns are not profiled.

Maintain a profiling findings log for each data source (a simple table in the catalog or a JIRA epic) recording: when the source was first profiled, what issues were found, how they were resolved, and what expectations were generated from the initial profile.
Document the profiling history table schema and the anomaly detection thresholds applied against it so on-call engineers can query it during an incident.
testingStrategies: Unit-test profiling functions with synthetic DataFrames that have known statistical properties (e.g., a column with exactly 5% nulls) and assert that the profiling output reports the correct values.

Integration-test profiling SQL queries against a sample of the real table in a staging environment to catch warehouse-dialect issues (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT syntax, REGEXP support) before the query runs in production.
Test the anomaly detection logic by injecting synthetic anomalies into the profiling history table (e.g., a sudden null-rate spike row) and verifying the anomaly detector fires the correct alert.

Backtest profiling-based thresholds against historical data: run the profiling anomaly detector over 90 days of historical metrics and verify it would have caught known past incidents without excessive false positives.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running a new query per column for each metric (N columns x M metrics = N*M warehouse queries).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers new to profiling write a loop over columns and issue individual SQL queries (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders, SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders, etc.) because it mirrors how they think about the problem column by column.
commonMistakes.impact: On a table with 50 columns and 10 metrics each, this generates 500 separate table scans instead of 1 — increasing warehouse cost by 500x, dramatically slowing profiling runtime, and overwhelming query concurrency limits.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Compute all per-column aggregate metrics in a single SQL query using multiple aggregate expressions separated by commas: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(col1), COUNT(DISTINCT col1), MIN(col2), MAX(col2), AVG(col2), COUNT(DISTINCT col2), ... FROM table. One scan, all metrics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Profiling without a partition filter, triggering expensive full-table historical scans for incremental checks.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Profiling is initially set up without partition awareness, and the engineer does not realize the table has years of historical data — the first production run scans all of it.
commonMistakes.impact: A profiling query against a 3-year-old orders table with 2 billion rows instead of today's 2 million new rows costs 1000x more and takes 10-50x longer, potentially timing out or generating unexpected warehouse bills.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always add WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day' (or the appropriate partition column filter) to incremental profiling queries. Run a full-table baseline scan only intentionally and on a low-frequency schedule (weekly/monthly). Check query scan cost estimates before running profiling queries on unfamiliar large tables.

commonMistakes.mistake: Including raw PII values in profiling top-N outputs stored to the catalog or sent in alerts.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Top-N value frequency analysis is a valuable profiling metric, and engineers apply it uniformly to all columns without considering that columns like customer_name, email, or SSN will return real sensitive values in the top-N list.
commonMistakes.impact: Real customer names, email addresses, or other PII appear in the data catalog, profiling dashboards, Slack alert messages, or profiling history tables — creating a compliance violation (GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA) and a potential data breach if those systems have broad access.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Maintain an explicit PII column exclusion list in the profiling configuration that skips top-N value output for sensitive columns. Apply hashing or truncation (first 3 characters + ***) to top-N values for semi-sensitive columns where frequency analysis is useful but exact values must not be stored. Review profiling output schemas with the security/privacy team before storing to catalog.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a one-time profile as a permanent baseline without refreshing it as the data evolves.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: An initial profiling run is used to set quality check thresholds and monitoring baselines, but the profiling is not scheduled to recur — the baselines reflect the data from six months ago.
commonMistakes.impact: As the business grows (more products, new markets, changed user behavior), the real data distribution shifts. The stale baseline causes monitoring thresholds to be wrong: expected null rates and cardinality values no longer match reality, leading to either persistent false-alarm alerts or missed quality issues that fall within outdated 'normal' ranges.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Run profiling on every new batch for critical columns (null rate, row count, distinct count) and persist metrics to a history table. Refresh expectations and anomaly detection baselines on a scheduled cadence (weekly or monthly) by re-running the profiler against recent data and comparing the new profile to the old one. Alert when a significant distribution shift is detected so the team consciously decides whether to update the baseline or investigate the change.

comparisonSection.feature: Profiling tool choice for interactive exploration vs. production pipelines
comparisonSection.explanation: ydata-profiling produces rich HTML reports with visualizations, correlation matrices, and missing-value heatmaps, making it ideal for exploratory work by a data scientist or engineer understanding a new dataset interactively. However, it pulls data into Python memory (expensive for large tables) and is not suitable for production on multi-GB+ DataFrames without sampling. Warehouse-native SQL profiling pushes all computation to the warehouse engine, scales to any table size, runs as a scheduled job, and has zero memory overhead outside the warehouse — making it the right choice for production pipelines and large tables. Both are complementary: use ydata-profiling for initial exploration, SQL profiling for recurring production profiling.

comparisonSection.feature: Cardinality estimation: exact COUNT DISTINCT vs. approximate HyperLogLog
comparisonSection.explanation: Exact COUNT DISTINCT guarantees a perfect answer but requires the warehouse to maintain or sort all distinct values internally, which is expensive (full scan + sort or hash) on high-cardinality columns in large tables. APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT uses HyperLogLog to estimate cardinality with approximately 1-2% relative error using fixed, small memory, and runs significantly faster and cheaper. For most profiling use cases — understanding cardinality class (low/medium/high), detecting cardinality anomalies, setting monitoring baselines — 1-2% error is completely acceptable. Use exact COUNT DISTINCT only when the profiling output feeds a uniqueness constraint that requires exact verification, and even then, consider validating the PK constraint separately with a targeted check rather than in the profiling pass.

comparisonSection.feature: Profiling schedule: one-time onboarding profile vs. continuous incremental profiling
comparisonSection.optionA: One-time profiling at data source onboarding
comparisonSection.optionB: Continuous incremental profiling on every batch
comparisonSection.explanation: A one-time profile establishes the initial baseline and is essential for data source onboarding and expectation generation, but it becomes stale as the source evolves. Continuous incremental profiling runs a lightweight column profile on each new batch, persists metrics to a history table, and enables trend analysis, drift detection, and anomaly detection over time. The cost of continuous profiling is low if the scan is partition-filtered to the incremental window. The two approaches serve different goals: onboarding profiling is comprehensive (all metrics, cross-column, cross-table) and one-time; production profiling is lightweight (key metrics only), incremental, and continuous. Mature data platforms use both: a thorough onboarding profile followed by continuous incremental profiling against the established baseline.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is data profiling and why is it important before building a data pipeline?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Data profiling is the systematic analysis of a dataset to compute descriptive statistics and structural patterns per column: null counts and rates, distinct values and cardinality, min/max/mean/stddev, quantiles, most-frequent values, data type inference, string length distribution, and format patterns. It is important before building a pipeline because it answers 'what is this data actually like?' before you commit to a design. Profiling reveals which columns can serve as join keys, what the realistic null rates are (so you can write accurate not-null checks), what value ranges exist (for range validations), what formats appear (for regex checks), and whether the data joins cleanly to existing tables. Without profiling, every threshold and constraint in your pipeline is a guess; with profiling, they are data-driven baselines.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: A strong answer names the key metrics computed (nulls, cardinality, min/max, distribution, top values, patterns) and articulates the connection between profiling and downstream quality checks — profiling is not just documentation, it is the input to check authoring and baseline setting. Mention at least one tool (ydata-profiling, SQL aggregate query, Great Expectations profiler).

beginnerQuestions.question: What is cardinality, and what does a high cardinality ratio vs. a low cardinality ratio tell you about a column?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Cardinality is the number of distinct values in a column. The cardinality ratio is distinct_count / row_count. A high cardinality ratio (close to 1.0) means almost every row has a unique value — this is typical of primary keys, UUIDs, transaction IDs, or timestamps. A low cardinality ratio (close to 0) means a small number of distinct values repeat across many rows — this is typical of status enums, country codes, boolean flags, or product category columns. Cardinality determines: whether a column can serve as a unique identifier (ratio = 1.0), whether it is suitable for indexing or partitioning, how to encode it in ML (label encode low-cardinality, hash-encode high-cardinality), and whether a uniqueness constraint is appropriate.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to see that you connect cardinality ratio to concrete engineering decisions: key detection, indexing, encoding, and constraint design. Also mention the edge case: a high-cardinality ratio in a small sample does not guarantee it holds in production data — profiling on a representative large sample is necessary.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does data profiling feed into data quality check authoring? Walk through an example.
intermediateQuestions.answer: Profiling provides the empirical observations that make quality check thresholds accurate rather than guessed. Example: you profile a new orders feed and observe that customer_id has a 3.2% null rate, amount has a min of -25 and max of 4999, and order_status has 6 distinct values. From this profile, you generate: (1) an expect_column_values_to_not_be_null on order_id (0% null — safe to assert), (2) an expect_column_null_rate_to_be_below on customer_id with threshold 5% (observed 3.2% + buffer), (3) an expect_column_values_to_be_between on amount from -30 to 5500 (observed range + buffer), and (4) an expect_column_values_to_be_in_set on order_status with the 6 observed values. Without profiling, these thresholds are guesses that either flap (too tight) or miss issues (too loose). Great Expectations' UserConfigurableProfiler and Amazon Deequ's ColumnProfilerRunner automate this translation from profile statistics to expectation suites.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A strong answer connects specific profiling metrics (null rate, min/max, distinct values) to specific check types (not_null, range, value_set), explains the buffer logic (observed value + margin), and names tools that automate the translation. Mention that profiling also establishes the anomaly detection baseline: the observed 3.2% null rate is the baseline against which a future null-rate spike is detected.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why are approximate algorithms like HyperLogLog used in production profiling, and what is the trade-off?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Exact COUNT DISTINCT on a large table (e.g., 500M rows) requires the warehouse to process all distinct values — typically requiring a full sort or large hash table — which is computationally expensive and may cost $10-50 per query in pay-per-scan warehouses. HyperLogLog (and its warehouse implementations: APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT in BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) uses a probabilistic data structure that computes cardinality with approximately 1-2% relative error using a fixed, small amount of memory regardless of data size, at a fraction of the compute cost. The trade-off is accuracy: HyperLogLog will report a 500M-row fully-unique column as having approximately 495M-505M distinct values rather than exactly 500M. For profiling use cases — cardinality classification, baseline setting, anomaly detection — 1-2% error is acceptable. The only scenario where exact COUNT DISTINCT is necessary is when the result directly determines whether a uniqueness constraint passes or fails, and even then, a targeted exact check on the primary key is better than paying for exact counting on all columns.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to see that you understand why approximate algorithms exist (cost, scale), can quantify the error (~1-2%), and know the specific warehouse functions. Bonus: mention t-digest for approximate quantiles and reservoir sampling for distribution estimation — same principle applied to other expensive exact computations.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you design a continuous data profiling system that detects distribution drift over time? What metrics would you track and how would you alert on anomalies?
advancedQuestions.answer: Design: on every new batch or daily partition, run a lightweight SQL profiling job that computes per-column: null_count, null_pct, approx_distinct_count, min, max, avg, stddev, and row_count. Write each metric as a row to a profiling_history table with columns (run_date, table_name, column_name, metric_name, metric_value). After each run, a downstream anomaly detection job queries the history table to compare today's metrics to the rolling 30-day baseline (mean ± N * stddev, or IQR-based bounds). Alert when: null_pct increases by more than 2 percentage points versus the 30-day average, distinct_count drops by more than 5% (cardinality collapse — may indicate deduplication or a broken generator), row_count deviates more than 20% from the 7-day moving average, or min/max values breach a hard static bound (amount < 0). Route alerts to the dataset owner with the column, the anomalous metric, today's value, and the expected range. Use whylogs or a similar profiling-over-time library for richer distribution comparison (Jensen-Shannon divergence on value distributions, not just scalar metrics). Tune sensitivity per column type: strict for ID columns (cardinality must not drop), loose for amount columns (stddev naturally varies).
advancedQuestions.explanation: This answer demonstrates end-to-end system design: profiling job design, history schema, anomaly detection algorithm, alert routing, and per-column sensitivity tuning. Interviewers also want to hear about scalability (partition filters, approximate metrics) and mention of a real tool like whylogs or Monte Carlo.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you use Amazon Deequ's ColumnProfilerRunner to profile a large Spark DataFrame and translate the results into quality constraints? What challenges arise at scale?
advancedQuestions.answer: Deequ's ColumnProfilerRunner.onData(df).run() computes approximate column statistics (null fraction, completeness, approximate distinct count, min/max/mean/stddev, histogram for categorical columns) for every column in one Spark job. The result is a ColumnProfiles object from which you extract per-column ColumnProfile instances: column_profile.completeness (1 - null_fraction), column_profile.approximateNumDistinctValues, column_profile.histogram for top values. Translating to constraints: extract completeness values and apply them as minimum completeness constraints (hasCompleteness(col, >= observed_completeness - 0.02)); extract approximate distinct counts and apply as minimum cardinality constraints for ID columns; extract histogram top values and apply as allowed values for enum columns. Challenges at scale: (1) Histogram computation on very high-cardinality columns (e.g., a 500M-row user_id column) creates very large histogram objects — limit to low-cardinality columns or use a top-N approximation. (2) The ColumnProfilerRunner does full-table scans — always filter the input DataFrame to the incremental partition before passing it. (3) Deequ runs on Spark, so cluster sizing and shuffle costs for columns with many distinct values need tuning. (4) Deequ's approxNumDistinctValues uses HyperLogLog internally, which is good for scale but means cardinality-based uniqueness assertions should use an explicit uniqueness constraint rather than relying on the approximate profile count.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A strong answer demonstrates familiarity with the Deequ API (ColumnProfilerRunner, ColumnProfiles, ColumnProfile attributes), explains the profiling -> constraint translation workflow, and identifies real scale challenges (histogram cost for high cardinality, partition filtering, shuffle). Interviewers testing Deequ knowledge want to see both API knowledge and practical gotchas.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your team is onboarding a new CRM data source. The vendor claims the data has a unique customer_id per row, all emails are populated, and status is always one of five values. Your initial profile shows: cardinality ratio on customer_id = 0.97 (not 1.0), email null rate = 8.3%, and status has 7 distinct values including 'legacy_active' which is not in the vendor's documentation. How do you proceed?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The three profiling findings directly contradict the vendor's claims: (1) cardinality ratio 0.97 means 3% of rows have non-unique customer_ids — potential duplicate records or soft deletes encoded as duplicate keys; (2) 8.3% email null rate means roughly 1 in 12 customers lacks an email — a problem if email is used as a join key or marketing target; (3) an undocumented 'legacy_active' status value will break pipelines that apply accepted_values validation against the 5 documented values. None of these are necessarily fatal, but all require resolution before the pipeline goes to production.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Step 1: quantify the duplicate customer_id issue — run SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM staging.crm GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to understand whether duplicates are 'exact row' duplicates (load error) or 'same ID, different rows' (e.g., a customer with multiple accounts or a CDC snapshot design). Share findings with the vendor. Step 2: investigate the 8.3% email nulls — are they concentrated in a specific segment (e.g., enterprise customers who didn't provide email)? If so, document as a known pattern and set the monitoring threshold to email null rate < 10%. If unexpected, raise with vendor. Step 3: get the vendor to document 'legacy_active' (is it a valid status for migrated records?) and update the accepted_values expectation to include it. Update pipeline documentation to explain the 7 statuses. Step 4: do not approve the pipeline for production until these three issues are resolved or explicitly accepted with documented risk. The profiling findings become blockers or documented exceptions in the onboarding sign-off.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a data profiling platform for a large enterprise with 500+ tables across multiple warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) and a data lake (S3/Parquet). The platform must automatically profile all new data arriving daily, detect distribution drift, populate a central data catalog with quality metadata, and alert dataset owners when anomalies are detected.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Architecture: (1) Metadata registry: a central table mapping each dataset to its warehouse/location, owner, profiling configuration (columns to include/exclude, PII exclusions, sampling rate, partition column, profiling cadence), and last-profiled timestamp. (2) Profiling job orchestration: an Airflow DAG per warehouse type generates and executes native profiling SQL (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT for Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift, approxCountDistinct for Spark on S3/Parquet) using warehouse-specific connectors. Jobs are triggered by table partition completion events or on a schedule. All profiling SQL is generated programmatically from information_schema metadata. (3) Profiling history store: a centralized Snowflake or BigQuery table storing (run_id, run_date, source_warehouse, table_name, column_name, metric_name, metric_value, is_approximate, row_count). (4) Anomaly detection service: a scheduled Python job queries the history table, computes 30-day rolling mean and stddev per (table, column, metric), and flags values outside mean ± 3*stddev or hard bounds. (5) Data catalog integration: after each profiling run, push per-column summaries (null_pct, distinct_count, min, max, top_values) to the catalog API (Datahub, Collibra, Alation). (6) Alerting: anomaly detector writes alerts to a queue (SNS, PagerDuty); each alert is routed to the dataset owner (from the metadata registry) with column, metric, today's value, and expected range.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Exact vs. approximate metrics: approximate (HLL, t-digest) for all tables > 10M rows; exact for small/critical tables. Full vs. incremental scan: incremental (partition filter) for daily profiling; full-table baseline on a weekly cadence. Push computation to each warehouse's native engine (minimize data movement) vs. pull to a central Spark cluster (consistent logic but data transfer cost). Schema-per-warehouse dialect handling adds engineering complexity but avoids expensive data movement.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition profiling jobs by table so each warehouse's profiling runs independently and can scale horizontally. Use warehouse-native compute (pushdown) to avoid data movement at scale. Batch wide tables (100+ columns) into groups of 20 columns per query to avoid single-query timeout limits. Implement priority tiers: critical tables profile on every batch; standard tables profile daily; low-priority tables profile weekly. Cache information_schema column lists per warehouse and refresh nightly rather than per profiling job.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Data profiling is the systematic per-column statistical analysis of a dataset — computing nulls, cardinality, distributions, patterns, and cross-column relationships — to understand data quality, bootstrap quality checks and monitoring baselines, and support data catalog documentation.
keyConcepts: Per-column metrics: null count / null_pct, distinct_count, cardinality_ratio (distinct/rows), min/max/mean/median/stddev, quantiles (p25/p75/p99), top-N values, string length distribution, regex pattern match %.

Three profiling layers: column profiling (single-column stats), cross-column profiling (correlations, functional dependencies, candidate keys), cross-table profiling (referential integrity, orphan rate, join-key overlap).
Approximate algorithms: HyperLogLog for APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (~1-2% error), t-digest / reservoir sampling for approximate quantiles — essential for scale.
Profiling -> quality checks: profiling results directly feed expectation thresholds (null rate + buffer -> mostly, observed value range -> be_between, observed distinct values -> be_in_set).
Continuous profiling: run per-batch incremental profiling and persist metrics to history table to enable drift detection and anomaly-based monitoring baselines.
commands: from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport; ProfileReport(df, title='Profile').to_file('profile.html')
profile.get_description()  # returns structured dict of all per-column stats
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT col), APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(col), MIN(col), MAX(col), AVG(col), STDDEV(col) FROM table WHERE dt = CURRENT_DATE
SELECT APPROXIMATE PERCENTILE_DISC(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col) FROM table  -- Redshift
SELECT APPROX_QUANTILES(col, 100)[OFFSET(95)] FROM table  -- BigQuery p95
interviewPoints: Profiling computes: nulls, cardinality, min/max/mean/stddev, quantiles, top-N values, string patterns, cross-column correlations/dependencies, cross-table referential integrity.
Profiling BEFORE writing checks — it makes thresholds data-driven, not guessed.
HyperLogLog (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT) for cardinality at scale: ~1-2% error, dramatically cheaper than exact COUNT DISTINCT.
Great Expectations UserConfigurableProfiler and Deequ ColumnProfilerRunner auto-generate expectation suites from profile statistics.
Continuous / incremental profiling + persisted history table = anomaly detection and drift monitoring baselines.
quickNotes: Always partition-filter profiling SQL: WHERE dt = CURRENT_DATE — never scan the full table history for an incremental profile.
Cardinality ratio near 1.0 = candidate key; near 0 = likely enum/categorical.
Top-N values reveal implicit enumerations, encoding anomalies (both NULL and 'N/A'), and value skew invisible to aggregate stats.
Functional dependency violations (zip_code -> city fails for 3% of rows) = data inconsistency, not just an anomaly.
Exclude PII columns from top-N output in profiling reports — top-5 values for a name column are real names.

keyTakeaways: Data profiling is the systematic per-column statistical analysis of a dataset — computing null rates, cardinality, min/max/mean/stddev, quantiles, top-N value frequencies, string length distributions, and format pattern matches — and is the mandatory first step before writing quality checks, setting monitoring thresholds, or building transformations on a new data source.

Profiling spans three layers: column profiling (single-column statistics), cross-column profiling (correlations, functional dependencies, candidate-key detection), and cross-table profiling (referential integrity and join-key overlap); all three are needed for a complete picture of a dataset's quality and join-ability.

Profiling results directly feed downstream quality activities: null rates set completeness check thresholds, observed distinct values populate accepted_values expectations, observed value ranges drive range checks, and cardinality ratios identify primary-key candidates — making expectations data-driven rather than guessed. Great Expectations' UserConfigurableProfiler and Amazon Deequ's ColumnProfilerRunner automate this translation.

At scale, approximate algorithms — HyperLogLog for cardinality (APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, ~1-2% error), t-digest and reservoir sampling for quantiles — are essential: exact COUNT DISTINCT on billion-row tables is cost-prohibitive, and 1-2% error is fully acceptable for profiling baselines and anomaly detection thresholds.

Continuous incremental profiling — running a lightweight column profile on each new batch and persisting per-column metrics to a time-series history table — converts profiling from a one-time onboarding activity into the real-time monitoring backbone that powers drift detection, anomaly-based alerting, and automatic baseline updates as data distributions evolve over time.
